CV-1.t: Describe how paired endocardial tubes from splanchnic mesoderm fuse into the primitive heart tube by the end of week 3 and loop to the right in week 4, and relate defective ciliary dynein (Kartagener syndrome) to dextrocardia.

Trace atrial septation through the septum primum, ostium primum, ostium secundum, septum secundum, and foramen ovale, and predict the defect when each step fails (patent foramen ovale, ostium secundum ASD, ostium primum ASD).
CV-1.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: atrial septal defect, patent foramen ovale

CV-1.t: Explain how fused endocardial cushions divide the atrioventricular canal and help form the membranous septum and the mitral and tricuspid valves, and relate endocardial cushion defects to Down syndrome.
CV-1.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: endocardial cushion defect

CV-1.t: Describe how neural crest cells build the spiral aorticopulmonary septum, and predict transposition of the great vessels from failed spiraling, persistent truncus arteriosus from failed septation, and tetralogy of Fallot from anterosuperior infundibular septum displacement.
CV-1.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: transposition of the great vessels, tetralogy of Fallot

CV-1.t: Trace fetal circulation through the umbilical vein, ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and umbilical arteries, and explain why the best oxygenated blood reaches the brain.

Explain closure of the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus at birth (falling pulmonary resistance, rising left atrial pressure, rising O2, falling prostaglandin E2) and name the adult remnants of fetal vessels.
CV-1.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: patent ductus arteriosus

CV-1.t: Relate the aortic arch derivatives (third arch to common and proximal internal carotid, fourth to aortic arch and right subclavian, sixth to proximal pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus) to the different paths of the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves.

CV-2.t: Describe the endocardium, myocardium, epicardium, and fibrous cardiac skeleton, and explain how the skeleton electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles except at the AV bundle.

Identify the features of cardiac muscle cells (branched, one or two central nuclei, intercalated discs with fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions, diads at the Z line) and contrast them with skeletal muscle.
Distinguish Purkinje fibers (large, pale, glycogen rich, few myofibrils, subendocardial) from working myocytes, and identify the atrial granules that store atrial natriuretic peptide.

Compare the tunica intima, media, and adventitia of elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles, continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal capillaries, and veins, and relate each wall structure to its function.

Identify endothelial products (nitric oxide, prostacyclin, endothelin-1, and von Willebrand factor and P-selectin stored in Weibel-Palade bodies) and predict how endothelial dysfunction shifts vessel tone and clotting.

CV-3.t: Locate the heart in the middle mediastinum with its apex at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, and identify the chambers that form the right border, left border, and anterior surface on a chest radiograph.

Relate chamber position to clinical findings: the right ventricle lies most anterior behind the sternum, and the left atrium lies most posterior against the esophagus, so left atrial enlargement can cause dysphagia.

Describe the fibrous and serous (parietal and visceral) pericardium and the transverse and oblique sinuses, and explain why pericardial pain refers to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).

Identify the great vessels (SVC, IVC, pulmonary trunk and arteries, four pulmonary veins, aortic arch branches from right to left) and the ligamentum arteriosum with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking under the arch.

Identify the internal features of each chamber (crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, fossa ovalis, coronary sinus opening, trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, moderator band, conus arteriosus) and compare left and right ventricular wall thickness.

Predict injuries from blunt and penetrating chest trauma: aortic tear at the isthmus near the ligamentum arteriosum after sudden deceleration, myocardial contusion, ventricular puncture, and hemopericardium causing tamponade.

CV-4.t: Identify the cusps of each heart valve, the anchoring of atrioventricular cusps by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, and the chest wall site where each valve is best heard.

Relate valve opening and closing to pressure differences across each phase of the Wiggers diagram (isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid and reduced filling, atrial systole) and to the timing of S1 and S2.

Interpret a left ventricular pressure-volume loop, identifying mitral and aortic valve opening and closing, and predict how the loop changes in aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, and mitral regurgitation.
Explain the jugular venous a, c, and v waves and x and y descents, and predict cannon a waves in AV dissociation and large v waves in tricuspid regurgitation.
CV-4.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: tricuspid valve disorders

CV-4.t: Explain physiologic, wide, fixed, and paradoxical splitting of S2 and give a cause of each (right bundle branch block or pulmonic stenosis, atrial septal defect, left bundle branch block or aortic stenosis).
Distinguish S3 (rapid filling of a volume-overloaded ventricle) from S4 (atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle), and identify functional flow murmurs in pregnancy, anemia, fever, and childhood.
CV-4.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: functional murmurs

CV-4.t: Classify murmurs by timing and location (systolic ejection, holosystolic, early diastolic, mid-diastolic, continuous), match each to its lesion, and predict changes with inspiration, squatting, handgrip, and Valsalva.

CV-5.t: Explain the phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential (fast Na+ upstroke, transient K+ outflow, L-type Ca2+ plateau, K+ repolarization, inward rectifier resting potential near -90 mV) and why the long refractory period prevents tetany.
Trace excitation-contraction coupling from T-tubule L-type Ca2+ channels through calcium-induced calcium release by ryanodine receptors (RyR2) to Ca2+ binding of troponin C and cross-bridge cycling.
Explain relaxation by SERCA (regulated by phospholamban), the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and the sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase, and predict why ATP loss in ischemia impairs both contraction and relaxation.
Explain how beta-1 adrenergic stimulation acts through cAMP and protein kinase A to phosphorylate L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban, and troponin I, raising contractility and speeding relaxation.
Explain the cardiac length-tension relationship at the sarcomere level (filament overlap and troponin C Ca2+ sensitivity) and contrast how force is graded in cardiac versus skeletal muscle.

CV-6.t: Calculate cardiac output, stroke volume, ejection fraction, and mean arterial pressure from given values, and use the Fick principle to calculate cardiac output from O2 consumption and arteriovenous O2 content.
Predict how changes in preload, afterload, and contractility alter stroke volume, end-systolic volume, and the position of the Frank-Starling curve.
CV-6.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: systolic and diastolic dysfunction

CV-6.t: Interpret combined cardiac function and venous return curves and predict the new operating point after hemorrhage, volume infusion, venoconstriction, increased contractility, or a change in total peripheral resistance.

Apply the law of Laplace to explain why concentric hypertrophy normalizes wall stress and a dilated ventricle needs more O2, and list the determinants of myocardial O2 demand (heart rate, contractility, wall stress).

Trace the baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus through CN IX, aortic arch through CN X, nucleus tractus solitarius) and predict heart rate and vascular resistance changes after standing, hemorrhage, and carotid sinus massage.
Explain hormonal control of blood volume and pressure by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, ADH, and the natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP.

Explain the mechanisms of orthostatic hypotension (volume depletion, autonomic failure such as diabetic neuropathy, prolonged bed rest) and define it as a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.

CV-7.t: Locate the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, trace an impulse through them, and explain why AV nodal delay allows the atria to finish filling the ventricles.
Explain the pacemaker action potential (funny current through HCN channels, T-type and L-type Ca2+ currents, K+ repolarization) and how norepinephrine and acetylcholine change the slope of phase 4.
Relate the blood supply of the SA and AV nodes (from the RCA in most hearts) to sinus bradycardia and AV block during an inferior myocardial infarction.
Interpret a normal ECG: identify the P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, T wave, and QT interval, calculate heart rate, and estimate the mean QRS axis from leads I and aVF.
Distinguish first degree, Mobitz I, Mobitz II, and third degree AV block and right and left bundle branch block on ECG, and predict which AV blocks arise in the AV node and which arise below it.
CV-7.usmle: Cardiovascular: Dysrhythmias: atrioventricular block, conduction disorders

CV-7.t: Identify premature beats, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, multifocal atrial tachycardia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes, and ventricular fibrillation on ECG, and relate each to its mechanism and risk of cardiac arrest.
CV-7.usmle: Cardiovascular: Dysrhythmias: premature beats, atrial fibrillation and flutter, tachycardias, cardiac arrest

CV-7.t: Explain how an accessory pathway in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome produces a short PR interval and delta wave, and describe sick sinus syndrome as SA node dysfunction causing sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or alternating bradycardia and tachycardia.
CV-7.usmle: Cardiovascular: Dysrhythmias: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, sick sinus syndrome

CV-8.t: Trace the origins and courses of the right coronary artery, left main, left anterior descending, and circumflex arteries, and identify the myocardial regions each supplies.

Define coronary dominance by the origin of the posterior descending artery and predict why the posteromedial papillary muscle, with its single supply, is the one that ruptures after an inferior infarction.
CV-8.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: complications of myocardial infarction

CV-8.t: Trace cardiac venous drainage through the great, middle, and small cardiac veins to the coronary sinus, and the anterior cardiac and smallest cardiac veins that bypass it.

Explain why left ventricular perfusion occurs mainly in diastole, why the myocardium extracts about 70% of arterial O2 at rest, and why tachycardia and high wall stress make the subendocardium ischemic first.
Explain local metabolic control of coronary flow by adenosine and other metabolites and why increased myocardial O2 demand must be met by increased flow rather than greater extraction.
Explain how an anomalous left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary artery causes myocardial ischemia in infancy once pulmonary artery pressure falls after birth.
CV-8.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: anomalous left coronary artery

CV-9.t: Identify the branches of the aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta, and abdominal aorta with their vertebral levels (celiac trunk T12, superior mesenteric L1, renal about L1, inferior mesenteric L3, bifurcation L4).
Trace the arterial supply of the brain through the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and identify the vessels that form the circle of Willis.

Trace the main arteries of the upper limb (subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial, ulnar) and lower limb (external iliac, femoral, popliteal, anterior and posterior tibial, fibular, dorsalis pedis) and locate the palpable pulse points.

Trace venous return through the SVC and IVC, the left renal vein crossing anterior to the aorta, and the hepatic portal vein, and identify the portosystemic anastomoses that dilate in portal hypertension.
Identify watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction, border zones between cerebral artery territories) and explain why they infarct first during systemic hypotension.
Compare the share of resting cardiac output received by the gut and liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, brain, and heart, and relate each to its O2 extraction.

CV-10.t: Describe the structure of lymphatic capillaries (blind ends, overlapping endothelial flaps, anchoring filaments) and explain how they return about 2 to 3 L of filtered fluid and protein to the blood each day.
Trace lymph from collecting vessels through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct to the left venous angle, and identify the regions drained by the right lymphatic duct.
Explain the forces that move lymph forward: valves, rhythmic contraction of lymphangions, the skeletal muscle pump, breathing, and rising interstitial fluid pressure.

Describe the structure and functions of lymph nodes, spleen (red and white pulp), thymus (cortex and medulla), and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, including where B and T cells mature and are selected.

Explain the causes and features of lymphedema (node dissection, radiation, tumor, Wuchereria bancrofti filariasis), including swelling that becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis develops, and chylothorax from thoracic duct injury.
CV-10.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Signs and symptoms: lymphedema

CV-11.t: Apply the relationship flow equals pressure gradient divided by resistance, and Poiseuille's law, to predict how changes in vessel radius, length, and blood viscosity alter resistance and flow.
Calculate total resistance for vessels arranged in series and in parallel, and explain why arterioles set total peripheral resistance and why parallel organ circuits can adjust flow independently.
Relate blood velocity to total cross-sectional area, and predict turbulence, bruits, and flow murmurs from Reynolds number factors such as anemia, high velocity, and stenosis.
Explain how arterial compliance and stroke volume set pulse pressure, and predict isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure from arterial stiffening with age.
Apply the Starling equation to predict edema from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, low plasma oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, or lymphatic obstruction.

Distinguish metabolic, myogenic, endothelial, neural, and hormonal control of arteriolar tone, and identify the main control of flow in the coronary, cerebral, skeletal muscle, skin, and pulmonary beds.

CV-12.t: Explain how central command and muscle mechanoreceptor and metaboreceptor reflexes start the exercise response, with early vagal withdrawal followed by rising sympathetic drive.
Predict changes in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, arteriovenous O2 difference, and O2 uptake during graded exercise using the Fick principle.
Explain the redistribution of cardiac output during exercise: metabolic dilation in active muscle, sympathetic constriction in gut and kidney, rising skin flow for heat loss, and stable brain flow.
Compare blood pressure and total peripheral resistance responses in dynamic (aerobic) exercise and static (isometric) exercise, and relate each to volume or pressure load on the heart.

Distinguish the trained endurance athlete's heart (eccentric remodeling, larger stroke volume, resting bradycardia from vagal tone, higher maximal O2 uptake) from pathologic hypertrophy such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

CV-13.t: Trace the exogenous and endogenous lipoprotein pathways (chylomicrons with apo B-48, VLDL, IDL, LDL with apo B-100, HDL with apo A-I) and the roles of lipoprotein lipase, apo C-II, apo E, LCAT, and CETP.

Classify familial dyslipidemias by defect and lipid pattern: lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II deficiency (type I, chylomicrons, pancreatitis), LDL receptor defects (type II), apo E2 (type III, remnants), and hepatic VLDL overproduction (type IV).
CV-13.usmle: Cardiovascular: Dyslipidemia: lipoprotein lipase deficiency, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperlipidemia

CV-13.t: Explain how HMG-CoA reductase controls cholesterol synthesis, how SREBP raises LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase expression when cell sterol is low, and how LDL enters cells by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

Explain the fuels of the heart (mostly fatty acid beta-oxidation through the carnitine shuttle at rest, plus glucose, lactate, and ketones) and the switch to anaerobic glycolysis with lactate build-up during ischemia.

Explain the role of thiamine pyrophosphate in pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and relate thiamine deficiency to wet beriberi (high-output heart failure, vasodilation, edema) in alcohol use disorder and malnutrition.
CV-13.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nutrition: thiamine deficiency, beriberi

CV-13.t: Explain how deficiency of B6, B12, or folate raises homocysteine and vascular risk, and how vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) and copper deficiency (lysyl oxidase, Menkes disease) weaken vessel walls.

Predict ECG changes of hypokalemia (U waves, flat T waves), hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS), hypocalcemia (long QT), and hypercalcemia (short QT), and relate hypomagnesemia to torsades de pointes.

CV-14.t: Explain the genetics of familial hypercholesterolemia: autosomal dominant LDLR, APOB, or gain-of-function PCSK9 variants, the gene-dosage difference between heterozygotes and homozygotes, and loss of feedback on liver cholesterol synthesis.
Relate hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3), myocyte disarray, and the variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance seen among relatives.
CV-14.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

CV-14.t: Relate Marfan syndrome (FBN1 on chromosome 15, increased TGF-beta signaling), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2), and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1) to aortic dilation, dissection, mitral valve prolapse, and arterial rupture.
CV-14.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

CV-14.t: Explain congenital long QT syndrome (loss of KCNQ1 or KCNH2, gain of SCN5A), compare Jervell and Lange-Nielsen and Romano-Ward inheritance, and relate Brugada syndrome (SCN5A loss) to sudden cardiac death.

Associate genetic syndromes with heart defects: Down syndrome (endocardial cushion defects), Turner syndrome (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation), 22q11.2 deletion (tetralogy, truncus arteriosus), Williams syndrome (supravalvular aortic stenosis), and VACTERL association.
CV-14.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Down syndrome, VATER/VACTERL association

CV-14.t: Relate Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin), Friedreich ataxia (frataxin GAA repeat), and mitochondrial DNA disorders with heteroplasmy (Kearns-Sayre syndrome) to cardiomyopathy or conduction block.

Explain why adult cardiomyocytes, which have largely left the cell cycle, respond to pressure or volume load by hypertrophy with reactivated fetal genes (ANP, BNP, beta-myosin heavy chain), and why infarcts heal by scar.

CV-15.t: Compare pressures and resistance in the pulmonary and systemic circuits, and explain how recruitment and distension lower pulmonary vascular resistance as cardiac output rises.
Contrast hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with hypoxic vasodilation in systemic arterioles, and predict pulmonary hypertension from chronic global hypoxia in COPD or at high altitude.
Explain how breathing changes venous return and ventricular filling, including normal S2 splitting, pulsus paradoxus, and the drop in cardiac output with positive pressure ventilation.

Predict pulmonary edema when pulmonary capillary pressure exceeds plasma oncotic pressure in left heart failure or mitral stenosis, and right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale) from chronic lung disease or pulmonary embolism.
CV-15.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: cor pulmonale, cardiogenic pulmonary edema

CV-15.t: Explain the gravity-dependent distribution of blood flow and ventilation from apex to base, the resulting V/Q ratios, and the conditions that create zone 1 (no flow).

Explain why hypoxemia from a right-to-left shunt barely improves with 100% O2, and identify nonrespiratory roles of the pulmonary circulation (ACE conversion of angiotensin I, bradykinin breakdown, filtering of small clots).

CV-16.t: Explain atherosclerosis as chronic inflammation: endothelial VCAM-1, monocyte and T-cell recruitment, oxidized LDL uptake by scavenger receptors into foam cells, IL-1 beta release, and metalloproteinases that thin the fibrous cap.
CV-16.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: atherosclerosis

CV-16.t: Explain acute rheumatic fever as molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal M protein and cardiac antigens, and identify Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells, pancarditis, ASO titers, and the Jones major criteria.
CV-16.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Acute rheumatic fever

CV-16.t: Classify vasculitides by immune mechanism: immune complex (polyarteritis nodosa with hepatitis B, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia), ANCA-associated (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA), and granulomatous T-cell (giant cell and Takayasu arteritis).
CV-16.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Autoimmune arteritis and vasculitis

CV-16.t: Explain immune-mediated pericardial, valvular, and conduction disease: Dressler syndrome after infarction, Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus, and congenital heart block from maternal anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies.
Distinguish hyperacute, acute cellular, acute antibody-mediated, and chronic heart transplant rejection (cardiac allograft vasculopathy) by immune mechanism and timing.

Describe how viral myocarditis moves from direct myocyte injury to a cytotoxic T-cell response and dilated cardiomyopathy, and identify eosinophilic hypersensitivity myocarditis and rare myocarditis after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination.
CV-16.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: myocarditis

CV-16.t: Explain how lost T-cell surveillance in AIDS or transplant immunosuppression lets HHV-8 driven Kaposi sarcoma grow and why lesions often regress when immunity returns, and relate atrial myxoma IL-6 release to fever and weight loss.

CV-17.t: Compare endocarditis bacteria by morphology and virulence factors: Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase, protein A, clumping factor), viridans streptococci (cocci in chains, alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant, dextran), Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus epidermidis (biofilm on prosthetic material).
CV-17.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: bacterial endocarditis

CV-17.t: Identify causes of culture-negative endocarditis (HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella) and relate Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis to colon cancer.
CV-17.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: bacterial endocarditis

CV-17.t: Describe the Trypanosoma cruzi life cycle (triatomine bug feces, nondividing blood trypomastigotes, intracellular amastigotes in heart and smooth muscle) and its transmission by transfusion, transplant, pregnancy, and food.

Describe Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete, Ixodes tick, white-footed mouse reservoir, OspA to OspC switching, VlsE variation) and Rickettsia rickettsii (Dermacentor tick, obligate intracellular, endothelial infection, actin-based spread).
CV-17.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious: Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever

CV-17.t: Compare flaviviruses (yellow fever, dengue; Aedes mosquitoes; positive-sense RNA) with filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg; negative-sense RNA; fruit bat reservoir; body fluid spread), and explain antibody-dependent enhancement in dengue.
CV-17.usmle: Blood & Lymphoreticular System: Infectious: dengue fever, Ebola virus; Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious: yellow fever

CV-17.t: Explain how coxsackie B virus (nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus, fecal-oral spread) enters cardiomyocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor and cleaves dystrophin with protease 2A, and name other myocarditis viruses (adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV-6).
CV-17.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: myocarditis

CV-17.t: Identify other microbial causes of heart and vessel disease: diphtheria toxin myocarditis, tuberculous constrictive pericarditis, and tertiary syphilis aortitis from obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.

CV-18-A.t: Define stage 1 (130 to 139 or 80 to 89 mmHg) and stage 2 (140/90 mmHg or higher) hypertension, and explain primary hypertension as polygenic with risk factors such as age, obesity, sodium intake, and alcohol.

Identify secondary causes of hypertension (renal artery stenosis from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, sleep apnea) and the key clue for each.

Describe hypertensive damage: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction and atrial enlargement, nephrosclerosis, retinopathy, and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms causing intracerebral hemorrhage.
CV-18-A.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: hypertensive heart disease

CV-18-A.t: Distinguish hypertensive emergency (severe elevation, often 180/120 mmHg or higher, with acute organ damage) from chronic hypertension, and identify hyperplastic onion-skin arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis.

Define pulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary artery pressure over 20 mmHg at rest) and classify its causes, including left heart disease (most common), lung disease and hypoxia, chronic thromboembolism, and heritable BMPR2 pulmonary arterial hypertension.
CV-18-A.usmle: Respiratory System: Pulmonary vascular disorders: pulmonary hypertension

CV-18-A.t: Explain pulmonary arterial hypertension pathogenesis (low NO and prostacyclin, high endothelin-1, smooth muscle proliferation, plexiform lesions) and predict a loud P2, right ventricular heave, right axis deviation, and cor pulmonale.

CV-18-B.t: Explain the causes of left-sided heart failure and relate pulmonary venous congestion to dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, basal crackles, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) in the lung.
CV-18-B.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: congestive heart failure

CV-18-B.t: Explain the causes of right-sided heart failure (most often left-sided failure; also cor pulmonale and right ventricular infarction) and relate systemic venous congestion to raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, pitting edema, and nutmeg liver.
CV-18-B.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: congestive heart failure

CV-18-B.t: Distinguish heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (40% or lower, systolic) from preserved ejection fraction (50% or higher, diastolic), and interpret an S3, raised BNP, and chest radiograph signs of congestion.
CV-18-B.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: systolic and diastolic dysfunction

CV-18-B.t: Explain how sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and ADH first support output but then drive fluid retention, remodeling, and progression, while natriuretic peptides partly oppose them.

Predict complications of heart failure: acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias, mural thrombi with embolism, cardiorenal syndrome, and cardiac cachexia.

Explain high-output heart failure in severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, arteriovenous fistula, wet beriberi, and Paget disease of bone, and contrast its low systemic vascular resistance with low-output failure.
CV-18-B.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: high-output heart failure

CV-18-B.t: Predict sudden cardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypotension from acute mitral regurgitation after rupture of chordae tendineae or a papillary muscle.
CV-18-B.usmle: Cardiovascular: Heart failure: chordae tendineae rupture, cardiogenic pulmonary edema

CV-18-C.t: Identify coronary atherosclerosis as the cause of most ischemic heart disease, list its risk factors, and name other causes (vasospasm, emboli, vasculitis, increased demand from tachycardia, hypertrophy, or aortic stenosis).
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: coronary artery disease

CV-18-C.t: Distinguish stable angina (fixed stenosis of about 70% or more, exertional, ST depression), unstable angina (plaque disruption with partial thrombus, rest pain, no troponin rise), and Prinzmetal angina (vasospasm, transient ST elevation).
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: stable and unstable angina, coronary artery spasm

CV-18-C.t: Trace the pathogenesis of myocardial infarction from plaque rupture and occlusive thrombus to irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 minutes, and distinguish transmural (often STEMI) from subendocardial (often NSTEMI) infarction.
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: acute coronary syndrome, myocardial infarction

CV-18-C.t: Predict the occluded coronary artery from ECG lead changes (LAD in V1 to V4; circumflex in I, aVL, V5, V6; RCA in II, III, aVF) and interpret the timing of troponin and CK-MB rise and fall.
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: myocardial infarction

CV-18-C.t: Relate the microscopic timeline of infarction (wavy fibers and coagulative necrosis in day 1, neutrophils at 1 to 3 days, macrophages at 3 to 7 days, granulation tissue by 1 to 2 weeks, scar by 2 months) to complications.
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: myocardial infarction

CV-18-C.t: Predict complications of infarction by timing: early arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock, fibrinous pericarditis, papillary muscle, septal, or free wall rupture (most often 3 to 7 days), ventricular aneurysm with mural thrombus, and Dressler syndrome.
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: complications of myocardial infarction

CV-18-C.t: Describe chronic ischemic heart disease (ischemic cardiomyopathy): healed infarct scars, hypertrophy of surviving myocardium, left ventricular dilation, progressive heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.
CV-18-C.usmle: Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease: coronary artery disease

CV-18-D.t: Explain the causes of aortic stenosis (age-related calcification, bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease) and its findings: crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids, pulsus parvus et tardus, concentric hypertrophy, syncope, angina, and dyspnea.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: aortic valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Explain the causes of aortic regurgitation (aortic root dilation from hypertension, Marfan, or syphilis; bicuspid valve; endocarditis; rheumatic disease) and its findings: early decrescendo diastolic murmur, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, eccentric hypertrophy.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: aortic valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Explain mitral stenosis (almost always rheumatic) and its findings: opening snap with diastolic rumble, left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation with mural thrombus, pulmonary hypertension, and dysphagia or hoarseness from atrial compression.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: mitral valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Explain the causes of mitral regurgitation (prolapse, papillary muscle ischemia or rupture, left ventricular dilation, rheumatic disease, endocarditis) and its holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, S3, and left atrial volume overload.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: mitral valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Distinguish acute (Staphylococcus aureus, normal valves) from subacute (viridans streptococci, damaged valves) infective endocarditis, identify the valves most involved, and interpret Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and splinter hemorrhages.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: bacterial endocarditis

CV-18-D.t: Distinguish nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis in cancer and hypercoagulable states and Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus (small sterile vegetations on either or both leaflet surfaces) from infective endocarditis.
CV-18-D.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis

CV-18-D.t: Explain mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration, links to Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, and ADPKD), its mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur that move earlier with standing or Valsalva, and its complications.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: mitral valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Explain how repeated rheumatic fever produces chronic rheumatic heart disease, with commissural fusion, thickened and shortened chordae, fish-mouth mitral stenosis, and combined mitral and aortic involvement.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: rheumatic heart disease

CV-18-D.t: Explain carcinoid heart disease: serotonin from liver metastases of a neuroendocrine tumor reaches the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis, while lung monoamine oxidase spares the left heart; urine 5-HIAA is high.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: tricuspid and pulmonic valve disorders

CV-18-D.t: Identify complications of prosthetic heart valves: valve thrombosis and embolism, mechanical hemolysis with schistocytes, structural failure of bioprosthetic valves, and endocarditis, often from Staphylococcus epidermidis.
CV-18-D.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: prosthetic valve complications

CV-18-E.t: Explain dilated cardiomyopathy causes (familial TTN variants, alcohol, prior myocarditis, doxorubicin, peripartum, Chagas, thiamine deficiency, hemochromatosis) and findings: four-chamber dilation, systolic dysfunction, S3, and functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.
CV-18-E.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: dilated cardiomyopathy

CV-18-E.t: Explain hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, outflow obstruction from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a murmur louder with Valsalva and softer with squatting, and sudden death in young athletes.
CV-18-E.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

CV-18-E.t: Explain restrictive cardiomyopathy causes (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis, Loeffler endocarditis) and its diastolic filling failure with right-sided congestion, and identify the low-voltage ECG despite a thick ventricular wall in amyloidosis.
CV-18-E.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: restrictive cardiomyopathy

CV-18-E.t: Compare dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy by chamber size, wall thickness, ejection fraction, and type of dysfunction (systolic versus diastolic).

Explain the causes of myocarditis (coxsackie B and other viruses, Chagas, Lyme, diphtheria, drug hypersensitivity, lupus, giant cell myocarditis) and its lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis, raised troponin, arrhythmia, and progression to dilated cardiomyopathy.
CV-18-E.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: myocarditis

CV-18-E.t: Explain stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, a catecholamine-linked transient apical ballooning with near-normal coronary arteries, usually in postmenopausal women after acute stress, and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy that improves once the rate is controlled.
CV-18-E.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the myocardium: takotsubo cardiomyopathy; Heart failure: tachycardia-induced

CV-18-F.t: Explain acute (primary) pericarditis, usually viral such as coxsackie B, and its sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
CV-18-F.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the pericardium: acute pericarditis

CV-18-F.t: Identify causes of secondary pericarditis (early post-infarction, Dressler syndrome, uremia, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, radiation, tuberculosis, bacteria, cancer, cardiac surgery) and match them to serous, fibrinous, purulent, hemorrhagic, or caseous exudate.
CV-18-F.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the pericardium: acute pericarditis

CV-18-F.t: Explain constrictive pericarditis (tuberculosis, prior viral pericarditis, surgery, radiation) and its Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, and calcification, and distinguish it from restrictive cardiomyopathy.
CV-18-F.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the pericardium: constrictive pericarditis

CV-18-F.t: Explain the causes of serous and hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and its findings (muffled heart sounds, low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans, enlarged globular heart on radiograph), and why the rate of fluid build-up matters more than volume.
CV-18-F.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the pericardium: pericardial effusion

CV-18-F.t: Explain cardiac tamponade, including traumatic or post-rupture hemopericardium, and predict Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus, and equal diastolic pressures in all chambers.
CV-18-F.usmle: Cardiovascular: Diseases of the pericardium: cardiac tamponade

CV-18-F.t: Identify metastatic disease as far more common than primary cardiac tumors, name the usual sources (lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma, leukemia), and relate pericardial spread to bloody effusion with malignant cells and tamponade.

CV-18-G.t: Explain left-to-right shunt physiology and Eisenmenger syndrome: pulmonary vascular remodeling raises pressure until the shunt reverses, causing late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults

CV-18-G.t: Explain ventricular septal defect (most often membranous) and predict its harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, the spontaneous closure of many small defects, and heart failure with large defects.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: ventricular septal defect

CV-18-G.t: Distinguish ostium secundum ASD (most common), ostium primum ASD (Down syndrome), and patent foramen ovale, and predict a fixed split S2, pulmonic flow murmur, and paradoxical embolism.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: atrial septal defect, patent foramen ovale

CV-18-G.t: Explain patent ductus arteriosus (sixth arch derivative; risk with prematurity and congenital rubella) and its continuous machine-like murmur, bounding pulses, and differential cyanosis of the toes once Eisenmenger syndrome develops.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: patent ductus arteriosus

CV-18-G.t: Explain tetralogy of Fallot (pulmonary infundibular stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, VSD) from anterosuperior infundibular septum displacement, its link to 22q11.2 deletion, boot-shaped heart, and relief of tet spells by squatting.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: tetralogy of Fallot

CV-18-G.t: Explain bicuspid aortic valve (about 1 to 2% of people, linked to Turner syndrome and coarctation) and predict early calcific aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, endocarditis, and ascending aortic dilation or dissection.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease: aortic valve disorders

CV-18-G.t: Explain coarctation of the aorta (linked to Turner syndrome and bicuspid valve) and predict arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses, and rib notching from enlarged intercostal collateral arteries.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: coarctation of the aorta

CV-18-G.t: Explain transposition of the great vessels (failed spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum, linked to maternal diabetes) and why survival depends on mixing through a PDA, ASD, or VSD.
CV-18-G.usmle: Cardiovascular: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults: transposition of the great vessels

CV-18-H.t: Apply Virchow triad to explain thrombus formation, distinguish pale arterial thrombi from red venous thrombi, identify lines of Zahn, and predict thrombus fates (propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization and recanalization).

Identify inherited hypercoagulable states (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C or S deficiency) and acquired ones (antiphospholipid syndrome, cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, immobility, surgery).
CV-18-H.usmle: Blood & Lymphoreticular System: Coagulation disorders: hypercoagulable states

CV-18-H.t: Classify emboli: venous thromboemboli to the lung, systemic emboli from mural thrombi to brain, legs, gut, kidney, and spleen, fat embolism 1 to 3 days after long-bone fracture, amniotic fluid embolism, and gas embolism.
CV-18-H.usmle: Cardiovascular: Vascular disorders: arterial embolism and thrombosis

CV-18-H.t: Distinguish white infarcts (solid organs with end-arterial supply) from red infarcts (venous occlusion, loose tissue, dual supply, reperfusion), coagulative from liquefactive necrosis, and the factors that decide infarct size.
Define petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis, and hematoma, and predict the effect of hemorrhage by volume and site, including shock after acute loss of more than about 20% of blood volume.
Distinguish transudate from exudate edema, relate each to Starling forces or inflammation, and contrast pitting edema with nonpitting edema of lymphedema.

Classify shock as hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, or distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) and predict cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure in each.
CV-18-H.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Shock: cardiogenic, hypovolemic, neurogenic, septic

CV-18-H.t: Explain the stages of shock (compensated, progressive with lactic acidosis, irreversible), septic shock mediators (endotoxin, TNF, IL-1, nitric oxide), and resulting multiorgan dysfunction (acute tubular necrosis, ARDS, DIC).
CV-18-H.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Shock: SIRS, multiorgan dysfunction, refractory shock

CV-18-I.t: Distinguish the three patterns of arteriosclerosis: atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis (hyaline and hyperplastic), and Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, which does not narrow the lumen.

Trace atherosclerosis from endothelial injury to fatty streak to fibrous plaque, identify the arteries most affected (abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal, carotid), and predict complications (rupture, thrombosis, embolism, aneurysm).
CV-18-I.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: atherosclerosis

CV-18-I.t: Explain familial hypercholesterolemia findings: LDL often above 190 mg/dL in heterozygotes, coronary disease in childhood or the teens in homozygotes, tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, and early corneal arcus.

Distinguish abdominal aortic aneurysm (atherosclerosis, older male smokers, infrarenal, rupture risk rising with diameter) from thoracic aneurysm (cystic medial degeneration, tertiary syphilis), berry aneurysms, and mycotic aneurysms.
CV-18-I.usmle: Cardiovascular: Vascular disorders: aortic and iliac aneurysm, rupture

CV-18-I.t: Explain aortic dissection (intimal tear into the media; hypertension, Marfan, bicuspid valve, Turner, cocaine), its tearing back pain, unequal arm pressures, widened mediastinum, Stanford A versus B, and complications such as tamponade and aortic regurgitation.

Explain peripheral arterial disease (claudication, rest pain, ulcers, ankle-brachial index 0.90 or lower, Leriche syndrome) and atheroembolic disease with blue toes and cholesterol clefts after arterial catheterization.
CV-18-I.usmle: Cardiovascular: Vascular disorders: claudication, aortoiliac disease, atheroembolic disease

CV-18-I.t: Explain pulmonary embolism from deep leg vein thrombi and predict sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia with raised A-a gradient, acute right ventricular strain, and why most emboli do not cause lung infarction.

Explain deep vein thrombosis risk factors through Virchow triad and its unilateral warm, swollen, painful leg, and distinguish it from superficial thrombophlebitis, including migratory thrombophlebitis with cancer (Trousseau sign).
CV-18-I.usmle: Cardiovascular: Vascular disorders: deep venous thrombosis, thrombophlebitis

CV-18-I.t: Explain varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency (incompetent valves, risk with age, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged standing) and predict edema, stasis dermatitis, and ulcers near the medial malleolus.
CV-18-I.usmle: Cardiovascular: Vascular disorders: varicose veins, venous insufficiency, stasis ulcers

CV-18-I.t: Distinguish primary Raynaud phenomenon (benign vasospasm in young women) from secondary Raynaud with scleroderma, lupus, or Buerger disease, and explain the white, blue, red color sequence.
CV-18-I.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Raynaud disease and syndrome

CV-18-I.t: Explain thromboangiitis obliterans (heavy smokers, often young men; segmental thrombosing inflammation of medium and small arteries extending to veins and nerves) and predict digital ulcers and gangrene unless tobacco use stops.

Explain giant cell arteritis (age over 50, granulomatous inflammation of carotid branches, headache, jaw claudication, high ESR, skip lesions on biopsy), its risk of blindness, and its link to polymyalgia rheumatica.
CV-18-I.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Polymyalgia rheumatica and temporal arteritis

CV-18-I.t: Explain Takayasu arteritis (granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aortic arch and branches, usually young Asian women) and predict weak upper limb pulses and unequal arm blood pressures.

Explain polyarteritis nodosa (hepatitis B link, transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium arteries with lesions of different ages, renal and mesenteric microaneurysms, lung sparing, ANCA negative).

Identify Kawasaki disease in a child under 5 (fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, swollen hands and feet, cervical lymphadenopathy) and predict coronary artery aneurysm as its key complication.

Distinguish ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, sinus, lung, and kidney), microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA, no granulomas), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (asthma, eosinophilia, MPO-ANCA).
CV-18-I.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome

CV-18-I.t: Identify IgA vasculitis (palpable purpura on buttocks and legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, IgA nephropathy, often after an upper respiratory infection in children) and Behcet syndrome (oral and genital ulcers, uveitis).
CV-18-I.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: IgA vasculitis, Behcet syndrome

CV-18-J.t: Distinguish capillary hemangioma, including the infantile (strawberry) type that appears in the first weeks of life, grows fast, regresses, and is GLUT1 positive, from cavernous hemangioma, which does not regress and is the most common benign liver tumor.

Distinguish pyogenic granuloma (including the pregnancy gingival form), cherry hemangioma, and bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella in immunocompromised hosts, neutrophilic infiltrate) from hemangiomas and Kaposi sarcoma.

Explain Kaposi sarcoma pathogenesis: HHV-8 infection, spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces, viral cyclin D homolog and LANA effects on p53 and Rb, and growth favored by immune suppression; lesions progress from patch to plaque to nodule.
Compare the classic, endemic African, transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated forms of Kaposi sarcoma by population, sites, and course.

Identify atrial myxoma as the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults (pedunculated, usually left atrial, ball-valve obstruction, emboli, constitutional symptoms) and cardiac rhabdomyoma with tuberous sclerosis in children.
Identify angiosarcoma risk factors (vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast for liver tumors; chronic lymphedema after mastectomy) and its aggressive course.

CV-18-K.t: Explain how bacteremia seeds damaged endothelium or fibrin-platelet deposits to form vegetations, and predict the likely organism by setting: native valve, IV drug use, prosthetic valve, dental work, or GI and GU procedures.
CV-18-K.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: bacterial endocarditis

CV-18-K.t: Predict complications of bacterial endocarditis: valve destruction and ring abscess, septic emboli (systemic in left-sided, lung in right-sided disease), immune complex glomerulonephritis, and mycotic aneurysm.
CV-18-K.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: bacterial endocarditis

CV-18-K.t: Distinguish acute Chagas disease (often mild; Romana sign) from chronic Chagas years later (dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and conduction block, megaesophagus, megacolon) in people from Latin America.

Distinguish the stages of Lyme disease (erythema migrans; then facial palsy, meningitis, and carditis with AV block; then large joint arthritis and late neurologic disease) and relate risk to Northeast and upper Midwest exposure.
CV-18-K.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious: Lyme disease

CV-18-K.t: Explain Rocky Mountain spotted fever as rickettsial vasculitis and predict fever, headache, a rash spreading from wrists and ankles to the trunk with palms and soles involved, thrombocytopenia, and possible shock and multiorgan failure.
CV-18-K.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious: Rocky Mountain spotted fever

CV-18-K.t: Compare yellow fever (midzonal liver necrosis, Councilman bodies, jaundice, black vomit) with dengue (fever, severe muscle and joint pain, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak in severe dengue).
CV-18-K.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Infectious: yellow fever; Blood & Lymphoreticular System: dengue fever

CV-18-K.t: Explain the shared mechanism of viral hemorrhagic fevers (endothelial damage, cytokine storm, consumptive coagulopathy) and the high fatality and body fluid spread of Ebola and Marburg filoviruses.
CV-18-K.usmle: Blood & Lymphoreticular System: Infectious: viral hemorrhagic fever, Ebola virus

CV-18-K.t: Predict viral myocarditis in a young adult after a respiratory or GI illness (chest pain, arrhythmia, raised troponin, heart failure) and identify lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis on biopsy.
CV-18-K.usmle: Cardiovascular: Infectious, immunologic, and inflammatory disorders: myocarditis

excluded.usmle: Cardiovascular: Adverse effects of drugs on the cardiovascular system (doxorubicin, sympathomimetic stimulants, ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, alpha blockers, minoxidil)
excluded.reason: Pharmacology and drug adverse effects are not on NPLEX Part I. Doxorubicin and cocaine are kept only as named causes of dilated cardiomyopathy, aortic dissection, and coronary vasospasm.
Device management is clinical practice, not biomedical science on NPLEX Part I.

excluded.usmle: Multisystem Processes & Disorders: Signs and symptoms (chest pain, palpitations, syncope, dizziness)
excluded.reason: Symptom work-up is clinical diagnosis; these findings are taught inside the condition objectives (angina, arrhythmias, aortic stenosis, orthostatic hypotension) rather than as separate objectives.
